title: Phase 0 scaffold built directly from init-source.plan.md, no code before the plan
detail: Executed plan §12 Phase 0 in full: root workspace, packages/scheduling-core's skeleton (frozen public surface as throwing stubs, value objects implemented and tested), apps/web's Next.js shell + Prisma schema + seed, the ported/trimmed AI-workflow apparatus (directives rewritten for Vitest+Next.js+SQLite instead of Jest+NestJS+Postgres, since scenario 01's versions assumed a stack this scenario deliberately doesn't use), the full docs/ADR set, and CI. Chose to leave scheduling-core's five pipeline stages as throwing stubs rather than empty shells or fake implementations — a stub that throws 'not implemented' is honest; a fake implementation that returns plausible-looking empty data would silently pass the wrong tests later. Phase 1 (the algorithm itself) is next.

title: init plan §7.2's calibration rule does not produce its own stated answer of N=18 — it produces N=15
detail: Plan §7.2 specifies suggestTransactionsPerStaff as a binary search for N where floorStaffHours(N) ~= targetUtilisation (0.8) x sum(maxWeeklyHours) (368) = 294.4, then asserts this 'yields N ~= 18 - 272 floor staff-hours against a 294-hour target'. Re-deriving floorStaffHours over N=8..40 from the committed CSV: N=15 gives 296 (off by 1.6), N=18 gives 272 (off by 22.4). N=15 wins under nearest, largest-N-with-floor-above, and smallest-N-with-floor-below. N=18 is the 5th-best candidate; the plan's own sentence states the 272-vs-294 mismatch without noticing it. This is load-bearing because 18 is @default(18) in prisma/schema.prisma, is in the shipped migration, and §7.8's entire seed demo is computed at it. Every other figure in §7.1/§7.2/§7.8 reproduced EXACTLY (112 cells, 3058 txns, all 7 rows x 4 columns of the calibration table, 46/34/38 seats, U_min=32 via sum(ceil(0.6*cap/8)) per staff rather than 0.6*368/8=27.6) - so the defect is isolated to this one derived claim, not to the measurement. Resolution options and the recommendation (ship 18, have suggest honestly return 15, explain the gap in ADR-0003) are in .ai/plans/phase-1-algorithm.plan.md D1/§2.0. Lesson: a plan that computes a table correctly can still state a wrong conclusion from it; re-derive the CONCLUSION, not just spot-check the table.

title: An executed plan is annotated in the successor plan, never edited in place
detail: Phase 0's agent proposed 'sua lai cau do trong plan §9/assumption 15' after finding that plan §9's 'no .env required (SQLite path has a default)' is technically false - Prisma's env("DATABASE_URL") has no default syntax, so a missing .env fails prisma generate with P1012. The diagnosis and the fix (commit apps/web/.env, negate it with !apps/web/.env in .gitignore) are both correct and verified in place. The proposed REMEDY is not: CLAUDE.md's Citation Protocol says 'Never retouch a plan after execution - leave the wrong prediction in and annotate it, that contradiction IS the evidence'. So init-source.plan.md §9 keeps its wrong sentence and phase-1-algorithm.plan.md §1 D3 carries the annotation. Corollary found while checking: the fix stopped at the .env file, and the stale 'no .env required' claim still survives in 4 places including the .env.example written by the same change (apps/web/.env.example:1, docs/09_running_it.md:11 and :29, readme.md:72, RUN.md:10). Reword to what is true - 'no .env to create; apps/web/.env ships committed' - rather than deleting the claim.

title: D1 resolved by the user: ship N=18 as the default, let suggestTransactionsPerStaff honestly return 15
detail: Chosen against two alternatives that were put on the table with their costs: (B) move the default to 15 - rejected because a new migration plus a re-derived §7.8 table would drop the demo's slack from 8 seats to 2 (32<37<44<46), a knife-edge outcome that could flip on an implementation detail; (C) retune targetUtilisation to ~0.74 so the formula outputs 18 - rejected as a constant reverse-engineered from its own answer. Option A costs no schema/migration/seed change, keeps the demo ordering comfortable (32<34<38<46), and turns the discrepancy into evidence rather than hiding it: ADR-0003 must state 'the data-driven suggestion is 15; we ship 18' with the reason being that N=15 commits 296 of 368 contracted hours to the floor alone, leaving nothing for the peak top-up or the rebalance pass to work with. Implication for Phase 1: suggestTransactionsPerStaff's tests assert 15 for the seed team, and that is NOT a bug against the @default(18) in schema.prisma - the two numbers are deliberately different and the README states both.

title: buildSchedulingInput extracted to application/shared/ -- both AutoScheduleHandler and AddAssignmentHandler must shape Prisma rows into SchedulingInput identically
detail: generateRoster (auto-schedule) and validateRoster (manual roster edit) both need the exact same SchedulingInput built from the same Schedule/StaffMember/Shift/DemandCell rows -- scheduling-core's own index.ts docstring warns about this class of drift for the FeasibilityGate itself ('one implementation of the rules, two callers ... a second copy is how the two paths drift'). The same risk exists one layer up, in the Prisma-row-to-SchedulingInput mapping, so it was factored into application/shared/build-scheduling-input.ts rather than duplicated when AddAssignmentHandler was added -- AutoScheduleHandler was refactored to call it too. Any FUTURE handler that needs a SchedulingInput (e.g. the coverage view) should call this helper, not re-derive the DemandGrid Map-building loop inline.

title: Coverage view recomputes Diagnostics LIVE from the persisted roster -- docs/04_data_model.md originally specified the opposite (read ScheduleRun.diagnostics), corrected once manual roster editing existed
detail: docs/04_data_model.md said the coverage view should read ScheduleRun.diagnostics (a stored snapshot from the last auto-schedule run) specifically to avoid recomputing something that might disagree with what the manager saw at generation time. That reasoning predates manual roster editing (AddAssignmentHandler/RemoveAssignmentHandler) -- once an assignment can be added/removed after the last run, the stored snapshot goes stale the instant the manager edits, and GetSummaryHandler had already made the opposite call for the summary report for the identical reason ('re-derives it from the persisted roster every time, so it stays correct after a manual edit'). GetCoverageHandler was built to match that existing precedent: it rebuilds RosterState by replaying detail.assignments through a fresh FeasibilityGate (same public surface generateRoster/validateRoster use -- computeRequiredStaff/computeShiftRequirements/FeasibilityGate/RosterState/buildDiagnostics, all already exported from scheduling-core's index.ts), then calls buildDiagnostics. Verified live: DELETE on one assignment dropped that hour's `scheduled` count on the very next GET .../coverage call, no auto-schedule re-run needed. docs/04's comment corrected in place with a dated note (not silently rewritten) rather than left contradicting the code -- any future read endpoint over the roster (not just coverage/summary) should default to this same live-recompute rule unless there's a specific reason to read a stored snapshot instead.

title: docs/adr/README.md's ADR index and its closing 'nothing is ported verbatim' line went stale the moment ADR-0005 was ported in Phase B, and nobody had reconciled the index since
detail: ADR-0005 (transaction-retry-boundary, ported from ../service-appointment-scheduler in Phase B) was added to docs/adr/ as a file but never added to docs/adr/README.md's index table -- and that file's own closing sentence ('Numbering starts at 0001 because nothing is ported verbatim... into this scenario's own ADRs') became factually false at the exact moment ADR-0005 landed, since it explicitly IS ported verbatim. This is the same class of gap as the naming_conventions.md/domain_modeling.md/zod_validation.md debt (directives/README.md, Phase F) -- a new pattern or file gets built without its OWN index/description being updated in the same task, even though the After-Task protocol says to. Fixed in Phase F. Lesson for future work: when porting or adding anything with its own index file (an ADR, a directive, a memory category), update the index in the SAME commit as the addition, not as a later doc-polish pass -- this is the second time in this repo's history that gap has been caught only in a dedicated reconciliation phase instead of when it was introduced.

title: Created ../_templates/ at the collection root -- canonical copies of the 3 directives that are genuinely stack-agnostic in mechanism (memory_sop.md, qa_standard.md, cqrs_pattern.md), to copy into future scenarios instead of retyping from memory
detail: User's suggestion, in response to finding real drift (cqrs_pattern.md missing, qa_standard.md pointing at a deleted directory) between what should have been near-identical files across the two scenarios in this collection. ../_templates/directives/ holds {{PLACEHOLDER}}-marked versions of exactly these three files -- NOT naming_conventions.md/domain_modeling.md/zod_validation.md/testing_standard.md, which are correctly scenario-specific in content even when their section headings rhyme; templating those would either produce something too generic to be useful or reintroduce the same copy-paste drift this folder exists to prevent. ../_templates/README.md documents the usage protocol explicitly: copy in, fill every {{PLACEHOLDER}}, add a provenance note, and -- the rule most likely to be forgotten -- port a REAL fix made in a scenario's copy back to the template in the same task, or the template regresses to worse-than-current and starts propagating the exact staleness it exists to prevent. This template folder itself is unproven until a third scenario actually uses it; treat it as a hypothesis about what reduces drift, not a guarantee, until that happens.

title: FIVE common directives were missing from this repo, not one: cqrs_pattern, folder_structure_sop, logging_standard, database_standard, observability_monitoring -- all ported in, plus idempotency_strategy kept as ⏸-not-needed rather than absent
detail: User corrected the model behind the earlier 'not ported, doesn't apply' calls: these are COMMON documents (Cortex -> service-appointment-scheduler -> here). Surplus is not wrong -- a scenario may not use a section, but it must not delete it, because a rule deleted for being unused is a rule nobody knows to re-add when it becomes relevant. Verified against the real code before porting, not assumed: prom-client/collectDefaultMetrics/`register` (observability), LogContext+createLogger+nestjs-pino across 8+ files (logging), 35 instances of @map/@default(uuid())/deletedAt (database), and eslint.config.mjs's own layer-boundary rules (folder_structure). All four genuinely apply NOW. The root cause of all five absences: init-source.plan.md §5 judged them inapplicable against the pre-reversal Next.js+SQLite stack, and NOTHING re-checked that judgment after the backend-architecture reversal reinstated NestJS/Postgres/CQRS/Docker -- the same stale-premise class as the CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md finding in the previous turn. Ported files keep scenario 01's exact section numbering so in-code `§N` citations stay valid; sections that don't apply here are marked ⏸ with a trigger instead of cut (observability §1/§3/§4 = Prometheus/Grafana deferred; idempotency = not needed by construction; folder_structure's idempotency//observability//value-objects//mappers slots = reserved-but-empty). Two places where copying verbatim would have been DANGEROUS and were adapted with the divergence stated inline: database_standard §5 (scenario 01 is Prisma 7 where `url` in the datasource block is an error; this repo pins Prisma 5 where it is REQUIRED -- copying sc01's text would have told an agent to break the schema) and §2's uuid(7) vs uuid() (v7 needs Prisma 6+).

title: Audited Cortex (distributed-social-platform) as the upstream root of the shared directives — it is CLEAN; every documentation defect found this session was introduced downstream in the port, not inherited
detail: Checks run against ../../distributed-social-platform: (1) every `directives/*.md` path referenced anywhere in its directives/docs/.ai resolves to a real file — the single apparent miss, `event_driven_sop.md`, appears only in two plans as a PROPOSAL ('cân nhắc thêm' = consider adding), correctly phrased as future work rather than a broken link; (2) its `directives/README.md` index lists all 18 directives, none unlisted; (3) every `docs/**.md` cited from a directive exists. So Cortex has better cross-reference hygiene than scenario 02 had before this session — the referenced-but-missing bug class was created in the Cortex→sc01→sc02 port chain, not propagated from the source. IMPORTANT context discovered: **Cortex's directives are written in Vietnamese** (16/19 contain Vietnamese prose); scenario 01 translated them to English when porting. This means a naive `diff` of section headings between Cortex and a scenario shows large fake 'dropped section' counts that are really translation artifacts (`## 📜 Luật Lệ (Rules)` → `## 📜 Rules`). The genuinely-dropped groups (naming_conventions' Guard/Caller/gRPC-Client; domain_modeling's entities-vs-aggregates; folder_structure's core-api-vs-auth-service comparison) were each dropped WITH a documented reason and a re-add trigger in scenario 01's own header — the discipline the user is asking for was already being followed at that boundary. Practical rule: when comparing a scenario's directive against Cortex, compare RULES not headings, because the language differs.

title: apps/web's mutation screens refresh via router.refresh() after every write, never local optimistic state -- one pattern across all six new screens (staff/demand/shifts/roster/summary/coverage)
detail: Every new screen's mutation handler (addStaff, updateShift, addAssignment, autoSchedule, ...) does: setPending(true) -> await the api-client call -> on success call next/navigation's router.refresh() (re-runs the Server Component's data fetch for the current route) -> on failure setError() for a Banner. No screen holds its own copy of server data that diverges from what getSchedule()/getSummary()/getCoverage() would return on a fresh load -- refresh() is the single re-fetch path, matching frontend_standard.md's rule that data fetching belongs in the server component, not client state. Chosen over optimistic UI updates because this is a single-user, single-process local app (assumption 14) where an extra round-trip is imperceptible, and because optimistic state would need its own reconciliation logic for the FeasibilityGate's 422s (an optimistic add can be REJECTED by the gate) -- refresh-after-confirm sidesteps that whole class of bug for a marginal latency cost. The one exception: RosterManager's drag-and-drop keeps the dragged assignment in the DOM until the destination add is confirmed successful, specifically so a gate-rejected drop leaves the original assignment in place rather than optimistically vanishing it.

title: GET /schedules/:id/suggested-n now 422s via a new InsufficientCalibrationDataError when staff, shifts, or demand cells are empty, instead of silently returning a near-meaningless N
detail: Traced the full call path (suggest-n.handler.ts -> buildSchedulingInput -> suggestTransactionsPerStaff in packages/scheduling-core) and confirmed every empty-input edge case (no staff, no shifts, no demand) was ALREADY crash-safe by construction -- computeRequiredStaff loops over an empty DemandGrid Map as a no-op, computeShiftRequirements pins closed-hour/zero-length-shift to floor=target=0 rather than NaN, and Prisma findMany returns [] never null/undefined. So this guard is NOT a defensive-against-a-crash fix; it exists because the algorithm silently degrades to bestN=1 (a number that looks legitimate but reflects zeroed-out math, not a real calibration) when one of the three inputs is missing. Chose to fail loudly (422, code INSUFFICIENT_CALIBRATION_DATA, details listing exactly which of {staff, shifts, demand} is missing) over returning 1 with no signal, because the UI's 'Suggest from data' affordance (docs/01 assumption 1) implies the number is trustworthy -- returning 1 without a flag would look like real data-driven advice. Deliberately scoped to suggested-n ONLY, not auto-schedule: generateRoster must never throw on feasible-but-bad input (CLAUDE.md hard rule) -- an empty roster + honest diagnostics is the correct auto-schedule behavior for missing data, whereas suggested-n has no diagnostics channel to carry that caveat, so 422 is the only way to signal it.

title: Split assignment/feasibility-gate.ts (155 lines) into eligibility-brand.ts + roster-state.ts + feasibility-gate.ts -- file organization only, still exactly 2 mutable classes
detail: User found the file hard to read: the Eligibility Symbol-branding trick, the RosterState class (7 methods), and the FeasibilityGate class (H1-H3) were all in one file, so reading a rule meant scrolling past unrelated branding-mechanics comments first. Considered converting scheduling-core to OOP generally, but rejected: directives/domain_modeling.md SS1 pins FeasibilityGate/RosterState as the ONLY mutable classes allowed in the package, specifically because index.prop-spec.ts property-based-proves H1-H3 never break -- that proof only holds because there is exactly one gate every assignment must pass through; adding more mutable classes risks a second mutation path and breaks the proof premise. Counted the package: ~36 total functions/methods but only 7 are on generateRoster's public pipeline path (computeRequiredStaff, computeShiftRequirements, FeasibilityGate.eligible, fairnessPass, coveragePass, rebalance, buildDiagnostics) -- the rest are private per-file helpers a reader only needs when debugging that specific stage, so neither OOP nor further file-splitting reduces function count; it only changed which functions sit next to which. Split: eligibility-brand.ts (the Symbol trick + Eligibility/EligibilityData types, read once), roster-state.ts (RosterState, the mutable accumulator), feasibility-gate.ts (trimmed to ~60 lines of pure H1-H3 rule logic, re-exports the other two so no external import site needed to change). Zero logic change -- 80/80 tests pass including the property-based flagship spec; typecheck and lint clean (pre-existing unrelated parserOptions lint errors on *.spec.ts files confirmed present on master via git stash before this change).

title: Bundled the always-together (gate, state) pair into one RosterContext value object, threaded through fairnessPass/coveragePass/rebalance/buildDiagnostics instead of two positional params
detail: User asked to reconsider directives/domain_modeling.md S1 ("no second mutable class") because manually threading gate+state through every stage function felt error-prone -- proposed wrapping the pipeline in an OOP class with this.state. Clarified the directive only forbids a SECOND MUTABLE class, not classes in general, so a thin orchestrator wrapping the existing FeasibilityGate/RosterState pair would not technically violate it -- but rejected the full-OOP path anyway: it would not have fixed the actual complaint (method-call ORDER is just as unenforced as function-call order; OOP does not add sequencing safety without a state machine), while costing a rewrite of 7 spec files (assigner.spec.ts, rebalancer.spec.ts, diagnostics.spec.ts, demand-model.spec.ts, shift-requirements.spec.ts, feasibility-gate.spec.ts, index.spec.ts all construct gate/state as plain values and call pure functions directly -- moving stages into instance methods breaks that per-stage unit-testability) and changing index.ts's "frozen at init" public surface (plan S2.3). Chose instead: RosterContext, a plain readonly interface { gate, state } -- NOT a class, so it does not add a mutable-class count and stays within S1's letter and spirit -- because gate and state are ALWAYS the same pair from the same SchedulingInput at every call site; bundling them removes the exact risk flagged earlier (a caller passing a gate from one input alongside a state from another) and halves stage-function arity (4-5 positional args down to 2-3) without touching per-function testability: a test still just writes an object literal, no constructor. generateRoster rebuilds the RosterContext (not mutates it in place) after rebalance(), the one stage that returns a NEW RosterState rather than mutating the existing one. Found and fixed a call site outside the package that would have silently broken: apps/scheduler-api's get-coverage.handler.ts calls buildDiagnostics directly with the old 5-arg signature -- caught by npm run typecheck --workspace=apps/scheduler-api failing after rebuilding scheduling-core's dist/ (apps/scheduler-api imports the built package, not src/, so typecheck must run AFTER npm run build --workspace=@scheduler/scheduling-core to see a scheduling-core signature change).

title: Role minimums (stretch goal) enforced as a seat-filling pass (rolePass), not a sixth FeasibilityGate constraint -- new ADR-0006
detail: The obvious first instinct given ADR-0001s H1-H4 precedent was a fifth/sixth gate case answering "may this candidate take this seat". Rejected: a role minimum answers a structurally different question ("is this seat legal yet, regardless of who"), and forcing it into FeasibilityGate.eligible breaks three things at once -- rebalancer.tss withoutAssignment throws on a previously-valid assignment that becomes infeasible on replay (exactly what happens removing a seats only supervisor), permutation-determinism (index.prop-spec.ts assertion 3b) breaks because a per-seat rule evaluated per-candidate depends on whos already committed which depends on iteration order, and Violation has no staffId-less shape for it. Chose instead: rolePass, a new stage in assigner.ts run FIRST in generateRoster (most-constrained-first -- a role minimum is the narrowest filter of any seat-filling rule, so filling it first makes a reported shortfall reflect genuine capacity lack not fill-order accident). FeasibilityGate/validateRoster are completely unchanged (D5) -- no new ReasonCode, no new gate case. Diagnostics.roleShortfalls (new required field) is the sole reporting surface, never thrown. rebalancer.ts gained roleCoverageDidNotFall alongside the existing coverageDidNotFall (which only compares per-seat COUNTS, so a swap can preserve headcount while destroying role coverage -- moving a shifts only supervisor to a non-required shift changes zero seat counts). Full reasoning: docs/adr/0006-role-requirements-as-seat-requirements.md.

title: User correction: the backend architecture is baseline engineering, not scope surplus — README now states scope explicitly instead of apologising for the stack
detail: I had been framing the NestJS/CQRS/Postgres backend defensively, repeatedly hedging it against the brief's 'do not gold-plate' line (section 9) and treating the public-repo/link questions as risks. The user corrected both premises directly: the company authorised a public repo, features only need to meet the stated requirements, and — the substantive point — architectural design is a baseline engineering competency, not decoration to be justified away. The fix they asked for was not to remove anything but to make the boundary explicit: a Scope section in the README naming what the brief required (all of sections 2.1-2.6 plus 5, with the verified numbers), and separately what went past it. The important distinction the section draws, and the one to preserve in future edits: the ARCHITECTURE is not the beyond-scope part — the brief leaves the stack open, so a domain layer and a real database are a decision rather than a requirement, but structuring seven features so the next developer can change them safely is ordinary engineering, and it costs the reviewer exactly one extra command. What IS genuinely beyond scope is enumerated honestly and separately: all five optional stretch goals (section 8), property-based testing, and the committed decision trail. Lesson for future sessions on this repo: do not re-litigate the stack against 'do not gold-plate', and do not describe the architecture as surplus in any document — state the scope boundary plainly and let the feature surface (which matches section 2 exactly, no more) carry the argument.
